input:
## Current use

In today's highly competitive industrial environment, understanding exactly how energy is used across a site is absolutely essential, and this assessment takes a comprehensive look at the energy picture at the paper mill in order to build a detailed picture of current consumption and to identify where meaningful savings might be achieved. The mill currently uses 1727 MWh of electricity per year, which represents a substantial quantity of energy by any measure. Of the various loads on the site, refrigeration stands out as taking the largest share of this electricity use, and it therefore deserves particular attention as the assessment unfolds. Alongside electricity, the mill also makes extensive use of steam, and both of these energy streams are considered in what follows, with a particular opportunity around heat recovery emerging as a central theme of the assessment. Energy touches every part of what the mill does, from the preparation of the stock through the forming and pressing of the sheet to the drying that finishes it, and the cost of that energy forms a significant part of the overall cost of production, so even relatively modest percentage improvements can be well worth pursuing in financial terms.

## Refrigeration

Refrigeration is, as noted above, the single largest consumer of electricity at the mill, and it plays a pivotal role in the site's day-to-day operations. The refrigeration plant runs compressors that remove heat from the areas and processes that require cooling, and that heat is ultimately rejected at the condensers, where it is simply given up and lost under current arrangements. This arrangement is interesting because it means that, at one and the same time, the site is spending heavily on electricity in order to throw heat away. The refrigeration load also has the advantage, from an energy-recovery standpoint, of running steadily throughout the year, since the cooling duty does not disappear with the changing seasons, and the chillers serve production areas whose cooling needs persist in summer and winter alike. It is precisely this combination of a large, steady cooling load and a continuous stream of rejected heat that makes the refrigeration plant such an attractive starting point when considering heat recovery on the site, and it forms the basis of the proposal that is developed later in this assessment. Sites of this kind typically spend a great deal on heating water and other process fluids at the very same time as their refrigeration plant is discarding heat, and it is this overlap, this simultaneous discarding and purchasing of heat, that heat recovery seeks to exploit by bringing the two sides together in a single, integrated arrangement.

## Steam

Steam is the mill's other major energy stream, and it is raised in boilers in order to supply the heat that the paper-making process demands, most notably for drying the sheet as it passes through the machine, as well as for heating process water and meeting a range of other heating duties around the site. The drying stage is particularly steam-hungry, since water has to be driven out of the sheet in large quantities, and the steam raised for it has to be available whenever the machine is running. It is important to note, however, that the steam figures available for this assessment are drawn from one winter month only, and this has significant implications for how confidently they can be used. Winter is the period when steam demand is at its most intense: incoming water is at its coldest, and heating requirements across the site are at their peak. Figures captured in such a month therefore risk overstating what steam demand looks like across a typical year as a whole, and they should be treated as seasonal rather than representative. This caveat is flagged here and carried forward into the recommendation, where it has a bearing on the decision that is ultimately reached.

## Recommendation

Bringing all of the strands together, the assessment has examined a possible heat-recovery retrofit in which heat rejected by the refrigeration plant would be captured and put to useful work elsewhere on the site. The retrofit is projected to save 20% of the mill's electricity use of 1727 MWh per year, which works out at a saving of 345 MWh per year. Using an electricity price of $0.12 per kWh, this translates into a financial saving of $41448 per year. Set against these savings, however, the capital cost of the retrofit comes in at $883k, and dividing the one by the other gives a simple payback period of 21.3 years, which is a very long time indeed. On top of this, it should not be forgotten that the steam side of the picture rests on figures from a single winter month, with all of the seasonal uncertainty that that entails. Taking everything into account, the prudent course of action would appear to be to hold back from committing the capital at this stage, and instead to gather a fuller picture of steam and refrigeration loads across an entire year before returning to the appraisal with firmer numbers on which to base a final decision. In the meantime, the opportunity itself is not in question, and nothing in this recommendation should be read as a judgement against heat recovery in principle, which remains an attractive prospect for the site in due course.

## Current use

The mill uses 1727 MWh of electricity per year, and refrigeration takes the largest share of that use. A heat-recovery retrofit on the refrigeration plant is the measure under assessment: it is projected to cut electricity use, but at a capital cost that the projected saving repays only over a long period, and the steam figures behind the assessment rest on one winter month. The recommendation is stated in full at the end of this assessment; the sections before it give the use figures, the refrigeration position, and the limit on the steam data.

Electricity is metered for the whole site, and the annual total is firm. The internal split between loads is less firm, because not every load is separately metered; the refrigeration share is the largest by the plant's own running records, and no figure in this assessment depends on the exact split. Electricity use follows production: the mill's drives, pumps, and refrigeration plant run when the machines run, and the annual total moves with the tonnage the mill makes. Steam is the second energy stream. Steam serves the drying of the sheet on the paper machine and the heating of process water, and its use is not metered as an annual total at all.

## Refrigeration

Refrigeration is the largest electricity load on the site, and it runs in every month of the year: the cooling duty follows production, not the weather. The refrigeration plant removes heat at its evaporators and rejects that heat at its condensers, where it is currently discharged and lost. A refrigeration plant of this kind is a heat source as well as a cooling source, and the rejected heat is steady because the load that produces it is steady.

The retrofit under assessment recovers heat at the condensers and delivers it to duties that are otherwise heated directly, preheating process water being the natural first duty on this site. A paper mill heats water in quantity: stock preparation, washing, and cleaning all draw hot water through the day, and each of those draws is a duty that recovered heat can serve in place of heat raised directly. The recovery does not change the cooling the plant provides; it changes the destination of heat the plant already moves. The limit on the scheme sits on the demand side: recovered heat has value only where a heated duty can take it at the time it is produced, and the assessment has not established that match hour by hour. Condenser heat is produced when the refrigeration plant runs, and hot water is drawn when production calls for it; the two patterns overlap on this site but have not been shown to coincide. The projected saving in the recommendation is therefore a projection from annual totals, not a metered result.

## Steam

Steam figures for the mill come from one winter month, and they are flagged here as seasonal. A winter month carries the year's coldest incoming water and its highest heating demand alongside the process load, so a winter month read as a typical month overstates steam use across the year. No annual steam figure is stated in this assessment, because none has been measured.

Steam serves the drying section, where it heats the cylinders over which the sheet passes and drives the water out of the sheet, and it serves process water heating across the mill. Both duties are production duties, and both run whenever the machine runs; the seasonal element sits in the incoming water temperature and in building heating, not in the process itself. That is what makes the winter figure treacherous: it mixes a steady process load, which a winter month represents fairly, with a seasonal load at its annual peak, and the two cannot be separated from one month's total.

The steam limit matters to the retrofit decision in one direction only. Heat recovery displaces heat that would otherwise be raised directly, and the value of the recovered heat depends on how much direct heating the site actually does over a year. A steam record built from a single winter month inflates that value. The electricity saving stands on metered data; the supporting steam picture does not, and the recommendation is written to keep the two apart.

## Recommendation

The retrofit is projected to save 20% of electricity use, a saving of 345 MWh per year on the metered base of 1727 MWh per year. At $0.12 per kWh the saving is $41448 per year, against a capital cost of $883k: a simple payback of 21.3 years. Mill management should not commit the capital on these figures. A payback of that length outruns the period over which either the tariff or the load can be forecast, and the case rests in part on steam data that one winter month cannot support.

The appraisal is a simple-payback appraisal, and its limits should be read with the figure. Simple payback charges the whole capital in the year it is spent and credits the saving at today's tariff in every year that follows; it allows nothing for the cost of the money, for maintenance of the new plant, or for the price of electricity moving in either direction. Those omissions do not rescue the case here. A case that fails on simple payback over a period of this length is not brought back by refinements that mostly charge it more, and the metering recommendation stands independently of them.

The next step belongs to the mill's energy manager: meter the steam system and the refrigeration load through a full year, and re-run the appraisal on the metered record. The metering should also resolve the question the annual totals leave open, whether recovered heat and heated demand coincide closely enough through the day for the projected saving to be collected in practice. Heat recovery at the condensers remains the candidate measure, and the refrigeration load that makes it attractive is not in question. What is missing is the annual evidence, and the decision should wait for it. If the metered record confirms the projection and the payback still stands where it stands now, the honest finding will be that the measure does not pay on energy savings at this site, and the assessment should be closed on that basis rather than carried forward on better hopes.
